solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: At sea crew initially persisted in bad manners

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word it follows
something at sea is confused and adrift, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: the first letter of crew
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A ship's crew kept up their rudeness all the way across the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: Disrespect is a lack of courtesy, so it is a synonym for rude behaviour or bad manners.

clue.text: Single-minded reactionary resolved to protect old volunteers

indicators.note: to protect something is to wrap it round, so one piece goes inside the other
a reactionary wants to go backwards, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: resolved, as in having made up one's mind
the Territorial Army, Britain's former name for its volunteer reserve force

explanation.surface: A determined right-winger has decided to stand up for elderly volunteers.
explanation.walkthrough: Reactionary governs everything before it, so the reversal comes last, after the volunteers are tucked inside. The Territorial Army was Britain's part-time reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: A dedicated person is wholly committed to one purpose, a synonym for single-minded.

clue.text: "Help!" victim called out

indicators.note: something called out is spoken, so we go by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: a sucker is a gullible victim of a con

explanation.surface: A victim of a crime shouts for help.
explanation.definitionFit: Succour is assistance given in time of need, a formal synonym for help as a noun.

clue.text: A politician drowning in beer and scotch

indicators.note: something drowning in a drink is submerged within it, so it sits inside

blocks.note: taken as written
a Member of Parliament
stout is a dark beer

explanation.surface: An MP is sinking into drink, beer chased with whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: Scotch looks like the whisky, but here it is the verb meaning to crush or put an end to.
explanation.definitionFit: To scotch a rumour or plan is to put an end to it decisively, the same as to stamp it out.

clue.text: Bitter at 27 time? This might help

definitions.text: Bitter at 27 time? This might help

blocks.note: surface reading: feeling resentful when it is time to stop working for good
setter's reading: bitter means bitterly cold, and 27 in its sense of hitting the sack means bedtime, so something that warms a cold bed

explanation.surface: Someone sour about being pensioned off might be consoled by this.
explanation.walkthrough: 27 across is read as going to bed, not leaving work, and bitter is the weather, not the mood.
explanation.definitionFit: An electric heated sheet laid on a mattress warms the bed on a freezing night.

clue.text: Blunder by scientist ultimately creating a monster

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word before it

blocks.note: the last letter of scientist
a blunder is a mistake

explanation.surface: A lab mistake ends with a scientist making a Frankenstein-style creature.
explanation.walkthrough: By means placed beside, so the scientist's letter comes first here.
explanation.definitionFit: A terror is a frightening person, often an unruly child, loosely a little monster.

clue.text: Bar allowed female to take up new position

indicators.note: a letter taking up a new position is moved from its place, here from front to back

blocks.note: free to do something means allowed to
names the letter that moves: F, the abbreviation for female, already the first letter of the word for allowed

explanation.surface: A pub or legal bar lets a woman move into a new job.
explanation.walkthrough: F is the abbreviation for female; it moves from the start of the word to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A reef is a ridge of rock or sand near the water's surface, which is one meaning of a bar at sea.

clue.text: A possible clue for when crude

blocks.note: surface reading: a hint about something, as a detective might find
setter's reading: the answer itself, read as an anagram signal plus four letters, is a clue whose solution is this little word

explanation.surface: A setter muses on how one might clue the word when, as though hunting for a hint.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: ROUGH works as an anagram signal and HEWN is its fodder, giving WHEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Rough-hewn means roughly shaped and unrefined, a synonym for crude.

clue.text: Seeing something, I cry out loud

indicators.note: out loud means spoken, so the sound of the words counts, not their spelling

blocks.note: to bawl is to cry noisily

explanation.surface: Someone sees something upsetting and sobs.
explanation.definitionFit: The eyeball is the organ we see with, so it is literally a seeing thing.

clue.text: Destroy with moving victory at beginning of winter

blocks.note: December 1st, written DEC 1, starts winter by the meteorologists' calendar; the 1 becomes I
in chess, mate is the winning move

explanation.surface: An emotional triumph as the winter season opens, set beside wrecking something.
explanation.walkthrough: Clue order is reversed: DEC 1 comes first in the answer. DEC is the calendar abbreviation for December, and the digit 1 stands in for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: To decimate is to destroy a large part of something, its common modern sense.

clue.text: The ways of one's ancestors, might one say?

indicators.note: asking how one might say it points to a word that is spoken, not written

blocks.note: one's roots are one's ancestry and origins

explanation.surface: A question about the traditions and customs of one's forebears.
explanation.walkthrough: In British speech route rhymes with root, so the two plurals sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Routes are paths or courses taken to a destination, plural synonyms for ways.

clue.text: Composer dropping in for something to eat

indicators.note: dropping means letting fall away, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: Frédéric Chopin, the Polish composer
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: A composer pops in for a bite.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping in looks like visiting, but it tells you to remove the word in.
explanation.definitionFit: A chop is a cut of meat such as lamb or pork, something to eat.

clue.text: P for Porsche fanatic?

blocks.note: surface reading: the letter in a spelling alphabet, P standing for Porsche
setter's reading: P is the opening letter of the fuel word, so the answer describes P, and it also names someone devoted to fast cars

explanation.surface: A spelling alphabet where P stands for Porsche, the kind a car enthusiast might devise.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the first letter of PETROL is P. The question mark marks the definition by example, since a petrolhead loves any fine car, not only Porsches.
explanation.definitionFit: A petrolhead is informal British slang for a car enthusiast, someone obsessed with motoring.

clue.text: Sailor's hat boy and I found in lake

indicators.note: something found in a place sits within it, so these go inside

blocks.note: a boy's name
taken as written
a tarn is a small mountain lake

explanation.surface: A sailor's cap belonging to a lad and the speaker turns up in a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: Sailor wants to give TAR or AB, but the whole of Sailor's hat is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarpaulin was a tarred or waterproof hat worn by seamen; the word also once meant the sailor himself.

clue.text: Papa alone, so I organised a dance

indicators.note: organised means put into a new order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: P is papa in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Dad is on his own, so the speaker throws a party with dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: The polonaise is a stately Polish processional dance, also the music written for it.

clue.text: Music producer's boss claiming £50

indicators.note: claiming something means taking hold of it, so it is held inside

blocks.note: chief executive officer
L is the abbreviation for a pound, from the Latin libra
L is fifty in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A record company chief demands fifty quid.
explanation.walkthrough: Music producer suggests a record label figure; here it is an instrument, which produces music.
explanation.definitionFit: A cello is a large bowed string instrument, a thing that produces music.

clue.text: Ask too much of English king in public

indicators.note: in places one piece within the other

blocks.note: the abbreviation for English
Latin for king
overt means done openly, in public view

explanation.surface: Expecting too much of an English monarch when he appears in public.
explanation.definitionFit: To overexert is to strain beyond one's capacity, demanding excessive effort of someone.

clue.text: Witness from trial, breaking schedule, turned up

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned up means read from bottom to top
breaking into something means getting inside it

blocks.note: a rota is a timetable of duties
a test is a trial

explanation.surface: A witness's evidence emerges after the court case disrupts the timetable.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the schedule is reversed; the trial goes into it afterwards. Turned up wants to mean appeared, as a witness might.
explanation.definitionFit: An attestor confirms something by formal statement or signature, a legal synonym for a witness.

clue.text: Bore with complaint on way back

indicators.note: back means going the opposite way, so the letters run right to left

blocks.note: Rd is the abbreviation for road, a way
an ill is an ailment or complaint

explanation.surface: A tedious person who moans about the journey home.
explanation.walkthrough: Bore looks like a dull person, but it is the verb, to make a hole.
explanation.definitionFit: To drill is to make a hole by boring, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: University terrified by head of department leaving

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
leaving means going away, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: dreading means fearing greatly
the first letter of department

explanation.surface: A university is frightened when a departmental head departs.
explanation.walkthrough: Terrified by means dreading, a slightly loose equivalence. Reading is a university town in Berkshire, west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The University of Reading is a British university, named after its town.

clue.text: Uncompromising student once having say about home

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the other

blocks.note: an old boy, a former pupil
to state is to say
at home means in

explanation.surface: A former student insists on having a voice in household matters.
explanation.definitionFit: An obstinate person stubbornly refuses to change their mind or yield.

clue.text: A cardinal holding island back? That's ludicrous

indicators.note: back means turned round, so the letters read the other way
holding means gripping within, so one piece sits inside

blocks.note: taken as written
IS is the abbreviation for island
a cardinal number, as opposed to an ordinal

explanation.surface: A prelate holding up an island's progress is called absurd.
explanation.walkthrough: Cardinal suggests a churchman; it is a number. The reversed island letters sit between A and NINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Asinine means foolish like an ass, a synonym for ludicrous.

clue.text: One generating a lot of interest?

definitions.text: One generating a lot of interest?

blocks.clueFragment: One generating a lot of interest?
blocks.note: surface reading: a fascinating person who attracts much attention

blocks.clueFragment: One generating a lot of interest?
blocks.note: setter's reading: interest is the money charged on a loan, and this person charges a great deal of it

explanation.definitionFit: A usurer lends money at extortionate rates, so their loans produce excessive interest.

clue.text: Regime in which Mary Poppins would feel at home?

blocks.clueFragment: Regime in which Mary Poppins would feel at home?
blocks.note: surface reading: a household or country where a magical childminder would be comfortable

blocks.clueFragment: Regime in which Mary Poppins would feel at home?
blocks.note: setter's reading: a government that interferes in people's lives like an overprotective childminder

explanation.walkthrough: Mary Poppins is the famous fictional nanny who looks after the Banks children.
explanation.definitionFit: A nanny state is a derogatory term for a government that is excessively protective and interfering.

clue.text: Sex before church is a sin

blocks.note: sex is Latin for six, VI in Roman numerals
the Church of England

explanation.surface: A moral pronouncement that sex before marriage is sinful.
explanation.walkthrough: Sex looks like intercourse but is the Latin number. Before simply places one piece ahead of the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A vice is an immoral habit or wickedness, a synonym for sin.

clue.text: High official, namely one accompanying queen

blocks.note: viz is the abbreviation for videlicet, meaning namely
Roman numeral one
Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: A senior official, that is to say one attending the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A vizier was a high-ranking minister in Muslim states such as the Ottoman Empire.

clue.text: Stupidly I take men a hallucinogen

indicators.note: doing something stupidly means doing it in a muddled way, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone foolishly offers men a mind-altering drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Ketamine is an anaesthetic drug also used recreationally for its hallucinatory effects.

clue.text: Nicaragua guerrilla nursing a fever

indicators.note: nursing means holding close, so the letters lie within the words before

blocks.note: spans the end of the country's name and the start of the fighter

explanation.surface: A Central American rebel fighter laid up with a fever.
explanation.walkthrough: Nursing suggests caring for the sick, which fits the fever, but it is the signal that the letters are held inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Ague is an old word for a malarial fever with fits of shivering.

clue.text: Stopping work and hitting the sack

blocks.note: first meaning: giving up one's job at the end of a career
second meaning: going to bed, from retire in its sense of withdrawing for the night

explanation.surface: Clocking off and going straight to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Hitting the sack looks like being fired from work, but it means going to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Retirement means both leaving employment for good and, more formally, withdrawing to bed.
